drops.label: Drop 1 - 10:10 AM ET: The app is a lead source, not an address
drops.theme: Keep the app. Own the address.
drops.headline: You do not have to leave the app.

copy.facebook_instagram:
No, you do not have to leave the booking app.

The version of this argument that ends with "so cancel your app" is wrong, and it is why a lot of people stop reading three paragraphs in. A channel that brings you paying work is not a problem. If an app is filling your calendar, the app is doing its job.

Here is the distinction worth holding on to.

An app is good at demand you did not create. Somebody opens it already intending to book somebody, and you are one of the options. That is real value and it is hard to replicate on your own.

A page of your own is good at demand you did create. Somebody heard your name, saw your work, got a referral, or searched for the specific thing you do. They need somewhere of yours to land.

Most barbers, braiders, nail techs and lash artists have both kinds of demand and only serve one of them. The second kind is the one currently evaporating.

The one thing worth moving is not your bookings. It is the ability to reach the people who already like your work.

Read it here: https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/do-you-have-to-leave-the-booking-app/

drops.label: Drop 2 - 6:00 PM ET: Booked solid, impossible to find
drops.headline: Booked solid. Impossible to find.

copy.facebook_instagram:
Someone new to your area searches for what you do. Your name does not come up.

Not because you are not good. Not because you are not busy. It does not come up because there is nothing of yours for a search engine to find: no page in your business name, no address of your own, nothing that exists outside one booking app and your messages.

This is not the same problem as app fees. You may know exactly what your app costs you every month and be perfectly fine with it. This is the quieter cost, and it never shows up on a statement.

People new to the area cannot find you. A move-in, a referral passed along without your handle, a search from somebody who does not already follow you - all of it goes to whoever appears in the results.

A stranger has no work of yours to browse. A marketplace profile shows a few photos in a fixed template. It does not show your range or your specialty.

And you own none of the traffic. Everyone who found you through the app found you through the app, so a change to how listings are ordered is a change to your income.

You are not missing bookings because you are bad at your job.

Read it here: https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/why-independent-stylists-are-invisible-outside-the-app/

drops.label: Drop 3 - 9:00 AM ET: Indexed is not the same as owned
drops.theme: Crawling, indexing, ranking - and whose domain it all accrues to
drops.headline: Google can find their page.

copy.facebook_instagram:
Does a search engine index your booking app profile? Usually, yes. And it still is not a web presence of your own.

Both halves of that sentence are true at the same time, and the gap between them is where work quietly goes missing.

Three words get used as if they mean the same thing, and they are three different steps. Crawling is a search engine following links around the web and reading pages. Indexing is filing a page it has read, so the page can be shown to somebody later. Ranking is deciding which of the filed pages to show first.

A marketplace profile usually clears the first two. Marketplaces want their pages read and filed, because that is how the marketplace gets found. So your profile is probably sitting in the index right now.

The trouble starts at the third step, and at a fourth thing nobody names. Every page on the web lives at an address, and the memorable part of that address - the yourbusiness.com part - is the domain. The domain is the unit search engines treat as an identity, and reputation accumulates to a domain over time.

Your profile lives on their domain. Every visit it earns and every link anyone points at it accrues to the platform.

Read it here: https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/does-google-index-your-booking-app-profile/

drops.label: Drop 4 - 7:00 PM ET: The price question that never becomes a message
drops.theme: The shop with no price tags
drops.headline: It is not the ninety seconds.

copy.facebook_instagram:
The message costs you more than the ninety seconds it takes to answer.

What it really costs is the bookings that never became a message at all, and those never show up anywhere you would notice them.

Picture a shop where nothing is priced. Everything in it is good and the owner knows the stock cold. But to learn what anything costs, you have to find the owner, wait out the person ahead of you, and ask out loud in front of strangers.

Some people will do it. Most will pick the item up, turn it over, put it back, and leave without speaking. The owner sees a quiet afternoon. What the owner does not see is the people who wanted to buy and would not ask.

A profile that says "DM for pricing" is that shop. Nothing about it is wrong or lazy. It is simply asking every interested stranger to do the one thing strangers are least willing to do.

Asking a price out loud is socially expensive. Reading one is free.

This is not an argument for ignoring your inbox. It is an argument about where the answer should live.

Read it here: https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/how-much-do-you-charge-dms-costs-bookings/

drops.label: Drop 5 - 11:00 AM ET: A permission is not a possession
drops.theme: What a client list actually is
drops.headline: A name you cannot reach.

copy.facebook_instagram:
You can usually see your client list. You can often export some version of it. You do not control it.

Access is a permission the platform grants you, and a permission is not the same thing as a possession. That is a practical description, not a legal one. What any specific platform may do with your data is set by the agreement you accepted, and the only reliable way to know yours is to read it.

The phrase "client list" sounds like a document. It is really four things, and platforms treat them very differently.

Identity - names, and how many of them there are.
Contact details - a phone number or an email address you could use to reach a person outside the app.
History - what they booked, when, how often.
Reach - whether you are permitted to contact them at all, and by what route.

Most people worry about the first one and feel fine, because the app shows a client count. The one that decides whether you have a business independent of the platform is the second, paired with the fourth.

A name you cannot reach is a memory, not a client list.

Read it here: https://famtasticdesigns.com/blog/who-owns-your-client-list-booking-app/

drops.label: Drop 6 - 10:10 AM ET: What a bookable page actually needs
drops.theme: Not a prettier profile - a different job
drops.headline: Not a prettier profile.

copy.facebook_instagram:
A page that gets you booked is not a prettier version of your app profile. It has a different job, because the person reading it arrived with a different question.

On a marketplace, a visitor has already decided to hire someone from that platform and is choosing between the listings in front of them. On your own page, a visitor is deciding something more basic: whether to hire you at all.

What that page actually needs:

Work grouped the way a client shops for it, not by the date you did it. Say what each piece is - "knotless box braids, mid-back, about five hours" tells a stranger more than a beautiful photograph with no caption.

A price or a range, and what it depends on. If you truly cannot post a number, post the thing that determines the number. Telling someone what the price depends on is itself an answer.

One obvious action, visible without scrolling on a phone.

Where you are, and whether you travel. This is the single most common reason a promising inquiry dies.

When you work, even approximately. And who you are, in two or three sentences in your own voice.

What you can skip on day one: the blog, the newsletter signup, the gallery that loads a hundred images.
